title: ENG-205 Sir Gawain Part 1 — 4 Main Ideas
subject: ENG-205

cards.def: At Camelot's New Year feast a giant, all-green knight dares Arthur's court to a "game" of one axe stroke now for one returned in a year and a day, and when no knight answers he mocks "the towering reputation of the Round Table," so the game is really a test of whether Arthur's court lives up to its fame for chivalry.

cards.term: Gawain takes the blow for Arthur
cards.def: When Arthur grabs the axe himself, Sir Gawain humbly asks to take the game instead, calling himself the "weakest" knight whose loss would be "least lamented," and after Gawain beheads him the Green Knight lifts his own head and orders Gawain to the Green Chapel next New Year "or be called a coward forever," so Gawain's courtesy and sworn word now bind him to seek his own death.

Before Gawain leaves Camelot the poet stops the story to explain the gold pentangle on Gawain's shield, an "endless knot" taken "as a token of fidelity" that suits Gawain because he is "fully faithful in five ways five times over," which makes truth (trouthe) the exact virtue the rest of the poem will test.

Gawain rides alone through a brutal winter, fighting beasts and giants while even the birds "pipe pitifully into the piercing cold," and only when Gawain prays to Mary on Christmas Eve does a castle appear, so the journey shows Gawain's isolation and hardship and his reliance on faith.

cards.term: The two promises at Bertilak's castle
cards.def: At the castle its lord (Bertilak) tells Gawain the Green Chapel is nearby, and Gawain swears "You may trust my tongue" and agrees to trade whatever he gains at the castle for "what I win in the woods," so the real test of Gawain's truth is quietly set up where Gawain does not expect it.
